stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents with a 12-hour history of high fever, persistent vomiting, severe headache, and increasing lethargy. She has no chronic medical problems. Her vital signs are: temperature 39.6°C (103.3°F), blood pressure 92/56 mm Hg, heart rate 148/min, and respirations 28/min. Physical examination reveals an ill-appearing, somnolent child who moans when moved. Neurological examination reveals marked nuchal rigidity with positive Brudzinski and Kernig signs; there are no focal neurological deficits, and funduscopic examination reveals sharp optic disc margins. Skin examination reveals multiple scattered petechiae and purpuric macules on the lower extremities and trunk. Two peripheral intravenous lines are rapidly secured, and blood cultures are drawn. A lumbar puncture is promptly performed without complication. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals: opening pressure 280 mm H2O, white blood cell count 3,200/mm³ with 92% neutrophils, protein 220 mg/dL, and glucose 18 mg/dL (serum glucose 105 mg/dL); Gram stain reveals numerous Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. In addition to initiating intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone, which of the following interventions is most appropriate to reduce the risk of long-term sensorineural hearing loss in this child?

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone only after completing 48 hours of bactericidal therapy
options.explanation: Corticosteroids given after antibiotic-mediated bacterial lysis has already occurred do not reduce neurological complications or hearing loss; timing must be prior to or concurrent with initial antibiotics.

options.text: Initiate continuous intravenous hypertonic 3% saline infusion targeting a serum sodium of 155 mEq/L
options.explanation: Hypertonic saline is reserved for impending cerebral herniation; prophylactic induction of severe hypernatremia is unnecessary and risks central pontine myelinolysis.

options.text: Perform repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures daily until CSF opening pressure normalizes
options.explanation: Serial daily lumbar punctures are not indicated for acute bacterial meningitis in children and increase infection and procedural trauma risks.

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone immediately prior to or with the first dose of antibiotics
options.explanation: This 3-year-old child presents with acute bacterial meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci; high CSF opening pressure, marked polymorphonuclear pleocytosis, high protein, and markedly low glucose < 40% of serum glucose). S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in children over 1 month of age and is associated with substantial rates of mortality and permanent morbidity, particularly sensorineural hearing loss (due to suppurative labyrinthitis and cochlear ossification). When bactericidal antibiotics lyse bacteria in the subarachnoid space, cell wall fragments (peptidoglycan and teichoic acid) trigger an explosive release of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1). INTRAVENOUS DEXAMETHASONE administered prior to or concurrently with the first dose of antibiotics blunts this subarachnoid inflammatory cascade, dramatically reducing the risk of permanent sensorineural hearing loss and neurological complications. If antibiotics have already been administered, adding steroids later confers little to no therapeutic benefit.

subject: Medicine
topic: Post-Cardiac Arrest Targeted Temperature Management
stem: A 56-year-old man collapses suddenly while jogging in a park. Bystanders immediately initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Emergency medical services arrive 6 minutes later and find the patient in ventricular fibrillation. The patient undergoes defibrillation twice, receives 1 mg of intravenous epinephrine and 300 mg of amiodarone, and achieves return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after 14 minutes of advanced cardiac life support. Upon arrival at the emergency department, the patient is intubated and mechanically ventilated. His vital signs are: temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F), blood pressure 114/74 mm Hg on a low-dose norepinephrine infusion, and heart rate 88/min. Neurological examination reveals an unconscious, comatose patient with Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3T; pupils are 3 mm and sluggishly reactive to light, corneal reflexes are intact bilaterally, and there is no purposeful movement or motor response to noxious sternal pressure. A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus rhythm with nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave changes, without ST-segment elevation or bundle branch block. Bedside echocardiogram shows global left ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 35%. Which of the following interventions has been proven to improve neurological outcomes in this patient?

options.text: Immediate administration of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone to reduce cerebral edema
options.explanation: Corticosteroids have shown no benefit in post-cardiac arrest hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and increase infection rates and glycemic instability.

options.text: Hyperventilation on mechanical ventilation targeting an arterial PaCO2 of 25 to 28 mm Hg
options.explanation: Inducing severe hypocapnia causes potent cerebral vasoconstriction, dangerously reducing cerebral blood flow and exacerbating ischemic brain injury.

options.text: Administration of 100% fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) targeting a PaO2 > 300 mm Hg
options.explanation: Severe hyperoxia promotes oxygen free radical generation and worsens reperfusion injury; oxygen should be titrated to an SpO2 of 92% to 98%.

options.text: Prophylactic administration of intravenous levetiracetam in the absence of electrographic seizures
options.explanation: Routine prophylactic antiseizure medication in non-convulsive post-cardiac arrest patients without documented electrographic seizures on continuous EEG is not recommended.

options.text: Initiation of targeted temperature management maintaining a constant core body temperature of 32°C to 36°C for 24 hours
options.explanation: Following return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, comatose adult patients (those who fail to follow commands or show purposeful responses) suffer severe ischemia-reperfusion brain injury. The standard of care to optimize cerebral recovery and improve survival with favorable functional neurological outcomes is TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT (TTM). TTM involves active cooling using surface pads or endovascular catheter devices to maintain a constant, controlled core body temperature between 32°C and 36°C (or actively preventing fever <= 37.5°C) for at least 24 hours, followed by controlled rewarming. Hypothermia and strict normothermia decrease cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen, attenuate post-ischemic cerebral edema, suppress glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, inhibit free radical generation, and block apoptosis cascades. Hyperthermia/fever must be strictly prevented, as every 1°C increase in body temperature above 37°C significantly worsens neuronal death.
